author: Rebecca Raney
title: Jury deliberations tentatively expected to begin Monday in triple murder, arson trial - NewsBreak
text:
By Rebecca Raney ,
41 minutes ago
After 3 1/2 days of testimony from nearly 50 witnesses, prosecutors could rest their case today against Johnny Ray Wilburn, 58, who is accused of killing three family members and setting fire to their Walland home.
Blount County District Attorney General Ryan Desmond confirmed Thursday that prosecutors expect to introduce Wilburn’s interviews with law enforcement this morning before concluding their case.
Once the interviews are introduced and attorneys have finished questioning Blount County Sheriff’s Office investigator Isaac Staley, defense attorney Rick Owens is expected to call several witnesses. Wilburn also will have the opportunity to testify on his own behalf if he chooses.
Judge David R. Duggan and attorneys tentatively expect to finalize jury instructions today, with closing arguments and deliberations scheduled to begin Monday.
By the end of Thursday’s proceedings, prosecutors had shifted from introducing and authenticating evidence to establishing a timeline of Wilburn’s movements and those of his associates before, during and after the killings.
Wilburn was arrested Jan. 21, 2025, in connection with the deaths of Cas Ivan Farley, 61; Delmar “Marty” Farley, 59; and Norma “Kaye” Farley, 65, and the destruction of their home on Payne Hollow Road.
The family’s two dogs and a cat also died in the fire, which a Tennessee Bureau of Investigation senior arson investigator testified Thursday was likely set to conceal evidence of the killings.
“In my expert opinion, this fire was likely set to serve as a forensic countermeasure in order to delay and deceive investigators, along with destroying evidence of various criminal activities,” investigator Don Cogan said.
Despite extensive burns to the victims’ bodies, Dr. Gayle Suzuki, deputy chief medical examiner at the Knox County Regional Forensic Center, determined that none of the Farleys died in the fire.
“One of the questions that we need to ask anytime we have a burned body is was this person alive prior to the fire? And so one of the things we look for is soot in the airways. If they’re still alive, they’re breathing in that soot,” Suzuki told jurors Tuesday.
None of the bodies had soot in their airways, she testified.
Investigators identified the victims through DNA comparisons. DNA recovered from the bodies was compared with a sample from one of Kaye’s living relatives and a tissue sample Marty had provided during his military service that was stored at the Armed Forces DNA Identification Laboratory.
After identifying Marty, investigators compared his DNA with that of the remaining unidentified victim, confirming he was Cas.
Suzuki testified that Cas died from a shotgun wound to the head and a probable stab wound to the heart. Kaye and Marty died from sharp-force injuries to the neck and chest.
Suzuki explained that such injuries can be caused by objects with sufficiently sharp edges.
Prosecutors also accuse Wilburn of stealing Marty’s debit card, shotgun and two safes containing personal documents, cash and handguns.
The firearms were later traced to Wilburn’s brother-in-law, Randy Pilkey, to whom Wilburn allegedly pawned them.
Surveillance footage showed Wilburn using the stolen debit card at a gas station, according to prosecutors. They also allege Wilburn and his on-again, off-again girlfriend, Kandice Cruze, used stolen cash and money obtained from Pilkey to make purchases at the Walmart in Alcoa on Jan. 19.
Prosecutors also presented surveillance footage from the Alcoa Inn, where Wilburn, Cruze and two friends stayed during the weekend of the killings.
Prosecutors contend that the surveillance footage, cellphone records and traffic camera data place Wilburn at locations consistent with their timeline of the murders and the disposal of evidence later recovered by investigators.
Owens, however, has maintained that the state’s case leaves room for reasonable doubt, arguing that much of the evidence is circumstantial and depends on prosecutors’ interpretation of events.
summary: After 3 1/2 days of testimony from nearly 50 witnesses, prosecutors could rest their case today against Johnny Ray Wilburn, 58, who is accused of killing three family members and setting fire to their Walland home. Blount County District Attorney General Ryan Desmond confirmed Thursday that prosecutors expect to introduce Wilburn’s interviews with law enforcement this morning before concluding their case. Despite extensive burns to the victims’ bodies, Dr. Gayle Suzuki, deputy chief medical examiner at the Knox County Regional Forensic Center, determined that none of the Farleys died in the fire.
